A symmetric extension of Zhao’s series for ζ⁡(5)\zeta(5)

Noam Shalev
Abstract

We prove a four-parameter extension of Zhao’s series for ζ⁡(5)\zeta(5). Restricting a Wilf–Zeilberger seed of Au to a hyperplane, we obtain a summand in five parameters with zero sum that is symmetric under all their permutations. Summing it from two different starting points gives two trigonometric closed forms, which we prove by Guillera’s periodicity argument. The proof is self-contained, and also gives a companion series for 1/π21/\pi^{2}, which we have not found in the literature. Specializing the parameters at roots of unity, we obtain Borwein–Bradley-type identities whose products depend only on x2x^{2}, x3x^{3}, x4x^{4} or x5x^{5}. Their Taylor coefficients are Apéry-like series for odd zeta values and for products of zeta values. In particular, we prove five identities conjectured by Au.

Keywords: Zhao’s series, ζ⁡(5)\zeta(5), Ramanujan-type series, WZ method, Borwein–Bradley identities, harmonic numbers

1 Introduction

Ramanujan’s series for 1/π1/\pi [1] have analogues for higher powers of π\pi. Guillera found and proved the first series for 1/π21/\pi^{2} [2, 3], and series for 1/π41/\pi^{4} were found by J. Cullen and by Y. Zhao (see the survey [4]). Guillera and Rogers [5] observed that inverting the Pochhammer quotient of such a series, which gives its upside-down counterpart, can produce a convergent series for a zeta value, even when the original series diverges. For instance, the Amdeberhan–Zeilberger series for ζ⁡(3)\zeta(3) [6] is the upside-down counterpart of a divergent series for 16/π216/\pi^{2} [7, (35)]. In the same way, Zhao found the identity [8]

∑n≥1an​p​(n)n9=−380928​ζ​(5),\sum_{n\geq 1}\frac{a_{n}\,p(n)}{n^{9}}=-380928\zeta(5), (1.1)

where

an\displaystyle a_{n} =(−10243125)n​(1)n9(12)n5​(15)n​(25)n​(35)n​(45)n,\displaystyle=\left(-\frac{1024}{3125}\right)^{n}\frac{(1)_{n}^{9}}{(\frac{1}{2})_{n}^{5}(\frac{1}{5})_{n}(\frac{2}{5})_{n}(\frac{3}{5})_{n}(\frac{4}{5})_{n}},
p⁡(n)\displaystyle p(n) =5532​n4−5600​n3+2275​n2−425​n+30.\displaystyle=5532n^{4}-5600n^{3}+2275n^{2}-425n+30.

Here (z)n=z(z+1)⋯(z+n−1)(z)_{n}=z(z+1)\cdots(z+n-1), with (z)0=1(z)_{0}=1, denotes the rising factorial. It is the upside-down counterpart of a divergent Ramanujan-like series for 1280/π41280/\pi^{4} (see [7]). Cohen and Guillera [4] list it next to the analogous series11 1 Curiously, its polynomial c⁡(n)≔483​n2−245​n+30c(n)\coloneqq 483n^{2}-245n+30 reappears in the coefficient of e22e_{2}^{2} of the polynomial PP (Section 2) and in the quadratic identity (3.1).

∑n≥1(−2563125)n​(1)n5(12)n​(15)n​(25)n​(35)n​(45)n​483​n2−245​n+30n5=−896​ζ​(3),\sum_{n\geq 1}\left(-\frac{256}{3125}\right)^{n}\frac{(1)_{n}^{5}}{(\tfrac{1}{2})_{n}(\tfrac{1}{5})_{n}(\tfrac{2}{5})_{n}(\tfrac{3}{5})_{n}(\tfrac{4}{5})_{n}}\frac{483n^{2}-245n+30}{n^{5}}=-896\,\zeta(3), (1.2)

conjectured by Guillera and proved by Au [9, Example IX]. It is remarked in [9] that (1.1) appears to be the only known hypergeometric series for ζ⁡(5)\zeta(5) whose terms decrease geometrically, and Broadhurst used it for record computations of ζ⁡(5)\zeta(5) [10]. A proof of (1.1) by a Wilf–Zeilberger seed is given in [9, Example X]; it combines the WZ pair with two further nontrivial evaluations, of a series equal to 2​(93​ζ​(5)−7​π2​ζ​(3))2(93\zeta(5)-7\pi^{2}\zeta(3)) and of a series for 14​ζ​(3)14\zeta(3). In [11, Example X], the seed gives a five-parameter family of series, whose Taylor coefficients lead to conjectural harmonic-number identities extending the same series.

In this short note, we study a four-parameter restriction of that family. In suitable coordinates, its summand is symmetric in five parameters whose sum is zero, and summing it from two different starting points gives two trigonometric closed forms (Theorem 1). The first leads to (1.1) (Corollary 2). The second gives a companion series for 1/π21/\pi^{2} (Corollary 3), which can be written as

∑n≥0(−1)n​(2n)!10(5n)!n!15(10n)!​3​(5532​n4+5464​n3+2173​n2+416​n+32)(10​n+1)​(10​n+3)=240π2.\sum_{n\geq 0}(-1)^{n}\frac{(2n)!^{10}\,(5n)!}{n!^{15}\,(10n)!}\,\frac{3\,(5532n^{4}+5464n^{3}+2173n^{2}+416n+32)}{(10n+1)(10n+3)}=\frac{240}{\pi^{2}}. (1.3)

Guillera’s bilateral sums [7, §5], [12] relate such convergent series to divergent ones, here to the divergent series for 1280/π41280/\pi^{4}. We have not found (1.3) in the literature. Specializations at roots of unity give Borwein–Bradley-type identities (Section 3), whose finite products depend only on x2x^{2}, x3x^{3}, x4x^{4} or x5x^{5}, as in Borwein and Bradley’s generating function for ζ⁡(4​n+3)\zeta(4n+3) [13, 14]. The quadratic and quartic ones generate ζ⁡(2​n+5)\zeta(2n+5) and ζ⁡(4​n+5)\zeta(4n+5), the cubic one generates ζ⁡(6​n+5)\zeta(6n+5) and π6​n+8\pi^{6n+8}, and the quintic one generates polynomials in ζ⁡(10​n+5)\zeta(10n+5) and π10\pi^{10}.

Comparing Taylor coefficients in these identities proves five of the six identities conjectured in [11, Example X]. A typical example is

∑n≥1ann9​[p⁡(n)​(11​H2​n(2)−7​Hn(2))+p7​(n)4​n2]=−3901440​ζ​(7),\sum_{n\geq 1}\frac{a_{n}}{n^{9}}\left[p(n)(11H_{2n}^{(2)}-7H_{n}^{(2)})+\frac{p_{7}(n)}{4n^{2}}\right]=-3901440\,\zeta(7), (1.4)

where Hn(r)=∑k=1nk−rH_{n}^{(r)}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}k^{-r} and p7​(n)=76632​n4−87620​n3+37835​n2−7225​n+510p_{7}(n)=76632n^{4}-87620n^{3}+37835n^{2}-7225n+510 (see Corollary 5).

The proof follows Guillera’s periodicity argument [7, 12, 15], applied to both sums together, and does not assume (1.1) or its companion.

3 Borwein–Bradley-type identities

Many Apéry-like series for zeta values are Taylor coefficients of identities whose summands contain finite products in one or more parameters. The first is the identity found independently by Koecher [17] and Leshchiner [18], which generates the values ζ⁡(2​n+3)\zeta(2n+3) and has Apéry’s series for ζ⁡(3)\zeta(3) as its constant term. Borwein and Bradley [13] found a generating function for ζ⁡(4​n+3)\zeta(4n+3) whose products depend only on x4x^{4}, later proved by Almkvist and Granville [14]. Bradley [19] and Rivoal [20] showed that both identities are specializations of a two-parameter identity conjectured by H. Cohen. Further identities of this kind were found by Bailey, Borwein and Bradley [21] and by the Hessami Pilehroods [22, 23], including a two-parameter extension of the Amdeberhan–Zeilberger series [23]. We call identities whose products depend only on one power xrx^{r} Borwein–Bradley-type. In [24], the series of Cullen and Zhao for 1/π41/\pi^{4} are constant terms of such identities with r=3,4,6,8r=3,4,6,8. Here, Zhao’s series (1.1) for ζ⁡(5)\zeta(5) is the constant term of such identities with r=2,3,4,5r=2,3,4,5.

We now restrict (2.7) to lines on which its finite products are products in one power of xx. Such lines come from roots of unity: if

θ=x⋅(1,ωr,…,ωrr−1,0,…,0),ωr=e2​π​i/r,2≤r≤5,\theta=x\cdot(1,\omega_{r},\ldots,\omega_{r}^{r-1},0,\ldots,0),\qquad\omega_{r}=e^{2\pi i/r},\qquad 2\leq r\leq 5,

then replacing xx by ωr​x\omega_{r}x permutes the coordinates. Therefore, every product over coordinates or pairs, and the polynomial PP, depends only on xrx^{r}. For r≤4r\leq 4 the line lies on e5=0e_{5}=0, so we recover the sum by perturbing the line and comparing coefficients in (2.7).

(Q−K)​(θ+z​r13)=O⁡((1+Y)D​e2​π​Y)(Q-K)(\theta+zr_{13})=O\bigl((1+Y)^{D}e^{2\pi Y}\bigr) (4.9)

for 0≤Re⁡z≤10\leq\operatorname{Re}z\leq 1. Hence its Fourier series contains only the terms e2​π​i​k​ze^{2\pi ikz} with |k|≤1|k|\leq 1, since the others grow faster than e2​π​Ye^{2\pi Y} at one end of the strip. Thus e2​π​i​z​(Q−K)​(θ+z​r13)e^{2\pi iz}(Q-K)(\theta+zr_{13}) is a polynomial of degree at most 22 in e2​π​i​ze^{2\pi iz}. On the other hand, by Lemma 6 and the first part of the proof, it vanishes where θ1+z∈ℤ\theta_{1}+z\in\mathbb{Z}, where θ3−z∈ℤ\theta_{3}-z\in\mathbb{Z}, and where θ1+θ2+z∈−12+ℤ\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}+z\in-\tfrac{1}{2}+\mathbb{Z}, that is, at three points that are distinct modulo 11. Therefore (Q−K)​(θ+z​r13)=0(Q-K)(\theta+zr_{13})=0, and Q=KQ=K on ℋ\mathcal{H}, as wished. ∎

Use of AI tools

The questions studied here and the restriction of the WZ seed to the hyperplane on which its summand becomes symmetric are the author’s. Large language models (Claude Opus 5.5 by Anthropic and GPT-6 by OpenAI) were used, under the author’s direction, for experiments with WZ seeds and to work out the proofs. The author checked all arguments, verified the certificate identity (4.2) and the coefficient comparisons of Section 3 by exact computation, and takes full responsibility for the paper.
